questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Agrarian Structure and Land Ownership' refers to.
questions.a: Indian rural society is organised around land: who owns it, who tills it, and who works on it for wages. The agrarian structure ranks people as landowners, tenant cultivators and landless labourers, and this ranking has shaped caste and class relations in villages for centuries.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Agrarian Structure and Land Ownership'.
questions.a: Ownership of land historically mapped onto caste hierarchies, with lower castes often confined to labouring on others' fields; land reforms attempted to break this bond between caste and land control.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Agrarian Structure and Land Ownership'.
questions.a: Describe the main strata of the agrarian structure in rural India.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Impact of Land Reforms' refers to.
questions.a: Land reforms after Independence aimed to abolish zamindari intermediaries, give tenancy security, and cap the size of holdings. Abolition of zamindari succeeded in breaking the old revenue-collecting class, while ceiling laws were weakened by transfers of land among relatives, and tenants often lost written records of their cultivation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Impact of Land Reforms'.
questions.a: Reforms redistributed some land to the tillers and ended hereditary intermediaries, but benefits flowed unevenly: owners of small plots and the landless gained least, and evasion of ceilings kept large operational holdings with dominant castes.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Impact of Land Reforms'.
questions.a: What were the three main aims of land reforms after Independence?

concepts.title: Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Green Revolution and its Social Consequences' refers to.
questions.a: The Green Revolution of the 1960s raised foodgrain output through high-yielding seeds, chemical fertilisers, irrigation and mechanisation, concentrated in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. Its social consequences included rising inequalities between big and small farmers, middle-caste landlord dominance, and environmental costs such as falling water tables and soil fatigue.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Green Revolution and its Social Consequences'.
questions.a: Regions and farmers with capital, assured irrigation and large holdings captured the gains first, widening regional and class disparities; mechanisation also reduced the demand for attached farm labour in some areas.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Green Revolution and its Social Consequences'.
questions.a: Name the regions where the Green Revolution first took hold.

concepts.title: Rural Transformations and New landed Groups

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Rural Transformations and New landed Groups' refers to.
questions.a: Post-reform rural society saw new groups rise: middle-caste farmers who used Green Revolution gains, state subsidies and political mobilisation to become dominant. Transformations include the spread of contract farming, diversification into dairying and horticulture, and the growing involvement of farmers' movements in price politics.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Rural Transformations and New landed Groups'.
questions.a: Rural change is not only about technology: credit access, state procurement prices and irrigation investments decided who gained, and the newly prosperous farmers turned economic strength into political clout.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Rural Transformations and New landed Groups'.
questions.a: Which caste groups rose to dominance in Green Revolution regions?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Circulation of Labour' refers to.
questions.a: Circulation of labour describes workers who migrate seasonally or cyclically between village and worksite, keeping their family base in the village while earning elsewhere. It differs from permanent migration: the worker returns for sowing and harvest, and employers prefer circulating workers because they can be paid less than settled urban workers need.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Circulation of Labour'.
questions.a: Circular migrants straddle two worlds: their wages subsidise farm households, while the village bears the cost of raising and schooling the labour the city employs. Industries from construction to brick kilns run on such circulating hands.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Circulation of Labour'.
questions.a: What is meant by circulation of labour?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Globalisation Liberalisation and Rural Society' refers to.
questions.a: Globalisation and liberalisation since 1991 reached the countryside through falling investment in agriculture, exposure to world price swings, and the entry of corporate agribusiness. Farmers faced rising input costs and unstable output prices, and agrarian distress grew into one of the period's central social problems.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Globalisation Liberalisation and Rural Society'.
questions.a: Rural India is not outside the global economy: crop choices, subsidies and trade rules decided abroad or in Delhi now shape village incomes, which is why farmer suicides and price movements became national debates.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Globalisation Liberalisation and Rural Society'.
questions.a: How did liberalisation affect public investment in agriculture?
